articles.description:
I wrote something down recently, and later I couldn't find it. If you know me, you know why; I put my notes into too many different apps.
Once in a while I declare loudly that "I'm using only this app, from now on! I mean it!" and then change my mind a month later. It's just the way I am. This most recent failure was the last straw and finally forced me to deal with it properly.
Instead of fixing myself, I built a software crutch. I spent today vibe-coding an indexer and search engine for all of my stuff. Here's the initial version of a web UI:

I also hacked together a TUI and an Emacs package. Those access the data via Tailscale SSH so I don't need to worry about installing things on other machines. Just the wrapper script.
Here's the list of sources being indexed (so far):
./archive index
baty.net: 1272 items (0.9s)
archive.baty.net: 2791 items (1.1s)
linux.baty.net: 26 items (0.0s)
blot.baty.net: 678 items (0.3s)
jackbaty.com: 581 items (0.1s)
notes: 2287 items (1.0s)
dayone: 2507 items (1.4s)
thebrain: 1177 items (0.5s)
mail: 1 updated, 0 removed (since revision 43773) (1.6s)
duplicates: 786 items in 381 groups (10.2s)

One nice thing about this is now I can search all of my Denote notes from my phone.
Everything is plain files and it uses boring, durable tools, so the archive should outlive whichever apps made the content that week. Even an AI layer, if I add one, sits on top of the search instead of being built into it. The database is disposable because it only takes 10 seconds to reindex everything.
Maybe now I'll be OK with all of my app churn.
✍️ Reply by email
articles.title: A searchable archive of everything

articles.description:
about debugging your init file. The main problem, he says, is that he sometimes makes a change that results in unbalanced parentheses. Often he doesn’t discover this until the next time he reboots Emacs, something he doesn’t do often.


He says that his usual method for finding the problem was to do what amounts to a binary search on his init file: He comments out half the init file. If the problem occurs, he repeats the process with the commented potion; otherwise he continues with the uncommented half. But then he discovered the built-in function check-parens that checks for unbalanced delimiters in the current buffer. That’s a nifty solution to Ridenour’s problem that I didn’t know about. Another tool in the toolbox.


The other thing about his post is that it reminded me of a package I wrote about in 2015 from Artur Malabarba: elisp-bug-hunter. I haven’t used it in a while but every time I do, it works perfectly and invariably finds the error often without any further action. What it does is automate the binary search that Ridenour used to hunt down his unbalanced parentheses but it works for any problem.


If the problem throws an error, elisp-bug-hunter will find it without any user input but for more complicated situations, you can specify a predicate to indicate whether the current run succeeded or not. I load it early in my init so it will be available if there is a problem.


So the take away from this post is two really useful debugging tools: check-parens for finding unbalanced delimiters and elisp-debug-hunter. Everyone should know these tools.
articles.title: Irreal: Debugging Init.el Files

People say that language is for communication, and every day Hacker News proves these people wrong.
I mean, it’s not just Hacker News, but it’s the place I encounter this phenomenon most often: Somebody will be discussing something, and then somebody else will respond with a short sentence that’s mostly acronyms.
The fascinating thing about these responses is that if you know what the acronyms mean, then what’s being stated is often trivial (i.e., something that everybody who knows what those acronyms mean already knows).  And if you don’t know what the acronyms mean, then the sentence is completely opaque.

articles.description:
has an interesting problem whose solution is harder than you think it would be. The problem is pretty simple: Every Sunday morning when he writes his weekly review, he needs to update all the clock tables in his journal. That usually takes about a minute and mbork had the idea that he could use an idle timer to run the update. Specifically, he reasoned that if Emacs were idle for a minute it probably meant that he was otherwise engaged and that Emacs would be idle for another minute so why not fire off his update?


Of course, he wanted to do this only once a week on Sundays so it was a bit more complex than just setting the idle timer. He came up with the idea of setting a (normal) timer for 3 AM on Sunday that would set the idle timer. That didn’t quite work because of a technical issue but he got things working with yet another timer.


You should read his post for the details. His solution is interesting and shows that sometimes even simple things can be harder than we imagined.
articles.title: Irreal: Updating Clock Tables

articles.description:
techhub.social, lispwizard has a short post (or whatever techhub.social calls them) on saving window configurations to registers. He notes how easy it is to save multiple configurations and switch between them on the fly.


Saving window configurations and other data in registers is an extraordinarily powerful technique that all Emacs users should learn and master. There’s a problem, though, when you want to do this programmatically: which register should you use? How can you be sure that your choice won’t conflict with a register that the user has chosen manually for some other task? There are several situations in which I want to run an Emacs function in a single window—Elfeed is an example—and I do that by saving the current window configuration, deleting the other windows, running the required function, and then restoring the previous window configuration but how do I choose a “safe” register to save the window configuration in?


The answer is a trick I learned from Magnar Sveen years ago. Instead of using a letter to name the register, you use a symbol like :saved-windows. That works because when you name a register with a letter, Emacs uses a pointer to its symbol as the register name. Using a symbol name like :saved-windows works because the result is also a symbol pointer.


If you have the need to save something in a register programmatically, this is a good way of doing it. You don’t have to worry about conflicts  because the user can not use symbol names for registers interactively.
articles.title: Irreal: Saving Window Configurations

a simple package that trades Org mode’s heading stars for UTF-8 bullets. If you’re like me, your first thought is, “Doesn’t that already exist?” Sort of. What already exists is the no longer maintained org-bullets. Cherti’s package is called org-ibullets (note the i).


Cherti explains the differences from org-bullets in his announcement. The TL;DR is that he’s optimized org-ibullets by eliminating redundant computations, eliminated spurious syntax warnings that org-bullets could produce, and made some improvements at the source level.


As I said, the package is simple. It can be used right out of the box but you can customize the list of bullets and their face if you desire. This seems like a very nice package if you’d like to make your Org buffers look a little nicer.

I came to realize that attempting to wrap up the “Wordcraft” section (as I call it) in Emacs is a fool’s errand. Emacs is Wordcraft. It’s what it’s all about. By the time I finish a draft, a new config or setting changes what I have. This here is an attempt to stay true to my conclusion in the last section.
Abbrevs
In my opinion, Abbrevs in Emacs is one of its fundamental features. It’s one of those things I’d show someone coming from other word-processing programs to show them the magic of Emacs. In essence, it’s a simple tool: you type two or more letters, and Emacs expands it to a phrase or even a whole paragraph. For example, when you type “hw” it will expand to “hello world” as soon as you hit space after the “w”.
Of course, you can achieve more with this useful function. We will get …

articles.description:
1. I did have this post from Curtis McHale about the future of Emacs interaction in my TODO queue so I decided to do a quick write up about it.


McHale’s contention is that we use keyboards because they’re the best way of interfacing with computers. He points to everybody’s favorite keyboard replacement, voice input, but notes that even on Star Trek—that arguably popularized the idea—Captain Picard still tells his crew members where he wants to go and they type in the commands at their control stations.


As I said in my last post on the matter. my written thoughts are always much better organized than my verbal ones so moving to spoken input would be a net loss for me. Still, it will be interesting to see how things play out.


Footnotes: 
1 



OK, OK. Maybe that overstates my usual efforts. I blame whatever sickness I have for that.
articles.title: Irreal: Will The Emacs Keyboard Die?

articles.description:
The moment general manager Chris Ballard was given Fredo's kiss by the Indianapolis Colts' HR department Monday morning, the rumor mill started to churn up replacements. This is bleak work, but consider that the alternative was analyzing how the Colts managed to lose at home against a previously winless Titans team on Sunday. The first name on that list, per Dan Patrick, was Peyton Manning. It's a perfectly silly, superficial, and absolutely in-play choice for the job: the only person who does insurance commercials more often than Flo from Progressive.
That's because Manning is the preeminent former Indianapolis Colt, a quarterback who won a Super Bowl ring for the team and had the best seasons of his Hall of Fame career in that town. It's in play because Manning is an omnipresent medioid who ably plays the affable goober, but is in real life anything but. It's also in play because the Colts are owned by the daughter of the late Jim Irsay, Carlie Irsay-Gordon, an owner who takes notes on the sidelines in a constant quest to avoid just being seen as another fail-offspring in a league that's lousy with them. After the team's final loss of last season, she asked Ballard if he believed he still had "his juju." Given that he got canned with a career record in the job of 72-82-1 and the Colts haven't reached the playoffs since the 2020 season, it puts a serious strain on the concept of "juju."
Somewhere in that notebook, at some point during Sunday's grim and lifeless 26-20 loss to the Tennessee Titans, for god's sake, Irsay-Gordon presumably wrote "this juju sucks," if not in so many words then decisively enough to punch Ballard's ticket. Irsay-Gordon explained her sideline note-taking thusly two weeks ago to Front Office Sports:
articles.title: Sometimes A Team Just Wants To Hire A Famous Guy

articles.author: Barry Petchesky
articles.description:
When last we checked in with Devin Cooley, he was serving as the backup goaltender for one of the worst teams in the league—I mean, downright putrid, couldn't-pay-me-to-watch bad. Not a lot has changed about the Calgary Flames in 11 months. They have two wins so far, second-fewest in the NHL. They have allowed 37 goals, second-most in the league. They're sporting a goal differential of minus-20 in just eight games played, which means that if you attend a Flames game, you should expect to see them lose by multiple goals. In practice they have lost multiple games by four, and multiple games by five.
It takes a type to thrive in that environment, and Cooley might be that type. All goalies are strange—they are under constant, ego-deforming pressure, and must spend an unhelpful amount of time alone in their own minds—but Cooley is rare in being able to describe his specific flavor of strange. In that interview last year, he displayed a mindset that while nihilist on its face, is probably pretty healthy in its ability to compartmentalize each save, each game, and wall it off from the saves and games he has yet to face. "Nothing matters," he said, "nobody cares, we're all going to die."
So, what would the Flames' poor 2026 start do for Cooley's mood? Well, ah, at least his bunny Tito seems in good spirits. Good for Tito. He's the only living being who can attend a Flames game and not suffer psychic damage.
articles.title: World’s Most Normal Goalie: “The Past Is Dead, There’s Nothing For You There”

articles.author: Patrick Redford
articles.description:
On Oct. 9, the New York Times reported that UFC veteran Tim Kennedy was recovering in the Walter Reed National Military Medical Center after he'd been shot three times while conducting a deadly, murkily defined operation with Erik Prince's private military group in the remote highlands of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo against Rwandan-backed rebel group M23. The constellation of proper nouns in that sentence is staggering, and lights the way to understanding the strange, idiosyncratic state of affairs in one of the most mineral-rich areas of the planet. I am going to walk you through this story, proper noun by proper noun (out of order), in hopes of untangling the messy web.
Democratic Republic of Congo
A few billion years ago, the large-scale geologic province known as the Congo Craton formed. Cratons are geologic provinces that have survived the endless churn of tectonic activity that recycles most of the Earth's crust, meaning they contain some of the most ancient rocks on the planet. In central Africa, the Congo Craton is overlaid by the massive and comparatively young Congo Basin, a sedimentary complex that contains the largest deposit of cobalt in the world, in addition to huge amounts of copper, gold, tantalum, and other valuable minerals.
articles.title: How Did A Famous, Lying UFC Vet Get Shot Conducting Shadowy Paramilitary Operations In The Congo?

articles.description:
Where the Sacramento Kings are concerned, all "joy" is relative. But this team, which projects to be among the NBA's worst, enjoyed one charming preseason storyline: the apparent revival of Ben Simmons as an actual rotation player. The basketball gods have chosen to deprive them and their fans of even this meager comfort. ESPN's Shams Charania reported on Sunday that Simmons tore his right Achilles tendon during a Kings practice, ending his season before it really began.
Simmons, a former All-NBA selection, went completely unsigned during the 2025-26 season. He deliberately distanced himself from basketball during that time, not even watching a game until the playoffs. That distance allowed the 30-year-old to pursue a maritime passion—sport fishing—and also allowed him to rebuild himself into a player good enough to sign the veteran minimum for a team projected by ESPN to win 21.7 games.
"I didn't touch a ball for the whole year," Simmons told reporters at Kings media day. "I didn't watch basketball. I just focused on getting my body right and my mind right." Multiple back surgeries had siphoned away his former athleticism. But Simmons observed a "night and day" difference in his mental health, after allowing his back to heal in his year off; affirmed his love of the sport; and, when asked if he could get back to his old self, said: "He's there. He woke up."
articles.title: Tiny Flame Of Joy Extinguished In Sacramento

articles.description:
For eons, roly-polies have rightfully dominated the rolling space, at least in our imagination. The crustaceans' astonishing ability to transform from a legged arthropod into a perfect sphere, a behavior called volvation, earned the bugs their nickname. But the bugs are far from the only rollers in the animal kingdom. Pangolins, hedgehogs, echidnas, and armadillos do it too, curling up their bodies into defensive balls. So does the Venezuelan pebble toad, which tucks in its head and tumbles down slopes to escape tarantulas. The Mount Lyell salamander rolls too, coiling itself into a wheel and bouncing down steep rocks. None of these animals become quite as Platonic a sphere as the roly-poly, but they do well enough.
But becoming a ball is not the only way to roll. The dwarf reed snake has found another way to roll away from danger, not by becoming a ball but by becoming something like a hoop. This peculiar motion, the mechanics of which are analyzed in a new paper in Current Biology, raises an important question: What is more sinister, a snake slithering in the grass or a snake rolling itself like a possessed wheel?
articles.title: Rolling Snakes Reinvent The Wheel

articles.author: Dave McKenna
articles.description:
Call it a buzzer beating. The reigning WBC super welterweight champ and most interesting man in boxing, Sebastian Fundora, delivered as interesting a knockout as memory serves while retaining his title Saturday night in Las Vegas. 
Fundora, the tallest 154-pound champ in history (6-foot-5.5 inches) and someone who taunts opponents about the ease with which he makes weight, wounded pesky challenger Ermal Hadribeaj with a vicious assortment of body blows and haymakers to the head as the last seconds of the last round of their brutal and surprisingly competitive 12-round slugfest ticked away. Then, just as the final bell sounded, Fundora landed a lightning-fast kill shot to Hadribeaj’s chin. Referee Thomas Taylor began counting out Hadribeaj, who was sprawled on the canvas, as most onlookers inside the casino arena were wondering what was going on, given that the clock had run out. 
But, no matter what the title of that ubiquitous '80s and ‘90s sitcom implies, you can no longer actually be saved by the bell in boxing, not even the bell ending the last round. And even though Hadribeaj got to his feet just before getting a 10 count, Taylor ruled he was in no condition to continue. And utilizing the powers vested in him by the so-called Unified Rules of Boxing, a package of uniform edicts which since around the turn of the century have been adopted in Nevada and throughout the U.S. that allows for fights to be stopped even after the final bell under such circumstances, Taylor waved his hands over his head and declared a knockout. (Decorated vets Terence Crawford and Tim Bradley, who sat ringside as working media for the TV broadcast, vented at Taylor after the fight for not letting Hadribeaj go home with a decision loss.)
articles.title: Nobody’s Having More Fun Than Sebastian Fundora

articles.author: Dave McKenna
articles.description:
Another new album of old Eva Cassidy recordings, called Jazzed, is about to come out. Cassidy, a peerless D.C. songbird, died 30 years ago next month. Her supply of unheard material ran out long ago. So those who legally control Cassidy's songbook transitioned from merely curating her art, as her label still claims to be doing with the latest project, to altering it. Jazzed gave me the blues.
Cassidy's talent was rare and huge, though it took her dying to get the music industry to notice. And the story of her quiet, relatively anonymous life giving way to massive posthumous popularity the world over is equally amazing. When she was alive and singing, Cassidy was unknown outside the D.C. area, where she was born and raised and stayed until the end. She really wasn't a big draw in her hometown, either. She had a small, hardcore group of local fans who loved her for her pitch-perfect voice and multi-genre musical range, and also for being a serene, sweet soul seemingly as oblivious to her own artistic genius as were all the record-label honchos who rejected her when she was knocking on doors looking for a deal. She paid her bills by working at a plant nursery, not by making beautiful music. Cassidy and her band gigged mostly at bars, never at theaters or music halls. She financed her own recordings, including 1996's Live at Blues Alley, the only solo album she lived to see released. 
But right when that record was about to come out, Cassidy began telling friends she wasn't feeling right, and died from melanoma mere months later. Some Cassidy recordings got into the hands of pop influencers in England in the late 1990s, most notably her cover of "Over the Rainbow," and over the next few years she became a phenomenon throughout Europe and then the world. Another big break came when Team USA's Michelle Kwan skated to Cassidy's version of "Fields of Gold" on the way to a bronze medal during the 2002 Olympics.
articles.title: There’s A Difference Between Honoring A Dead Artist And Exploiting One

articles.description:
We recently moved from a rural suburb in Massachusetts to a small coastal village in Rhode Island.
It’s been transformative, and I wish I’d done it sooner!
Trickle-Down Effects Unlike a city, a village has homes with yards. Unlike a suburb, a village has businesses and parks intermixed with homes. It’s the best of both worlds.
Being able to walk or bike places has trickle-down effects.
 Instead of driving 20 minutes one-way to get groceries, I can ride my bike there in 5 minutes.
articles.title: Life on Foot

articles.description:
About 14 years ago, we moved out into the rural suburbs. I loved the quiet, the abundant wildlife, and our proximity to farms.
I didn’t realize just how often doing anything at all would require a car.
The Sprawl Absolutely nothing was walkable. We lived at the very top of a very high hill, so things weren’t really bikeable either.
Groceries, restaurants, entertainment, friends, the library, and so on… you need to get in a car and drive at least 15 minutes for all of it.
articles.title: The Village

articles.description:
I saw this on Mastodon today (saved the image, lost the source), and it just brought me so much joy!
 Did you know that we live in a world where octopuses dream, otters have a favorite shell that they carry with them all their lives, cows have best friends, and bees have different “dialects” of dance depending on the region?
Or that cats purr at a frequency that accelerates bone healing, the forest grows flowers first after a fire, and dolphins give each other names and respond to them, and Penguins make proposals by giving each other the most beautiful pebble?
